question:
Patient note:
A 30-year-old man is reviewed on the morning of surgery while lying supine in the high-dependency bay awaiting transfer to theatre for a planned three-port laparoscopic resection of a chronically inflamed terminal ileal segment complicated by fistulising Crohn disease. He was admitted nine days ago from the emergency department with high-grade fever, rigors, diffuse abdominal pain, and tachycardia; blood cultures drawn at that time later yielded Gram-negative enteric bacilli sensitive to piperacillin-tazobactam, and abdominal CT demonstrated a 4-cm walled-off abscess in the right lower quadrant adjacent to the diseased bowel loop. Broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics, percutaneous drainage, and aggressive fluid resuscitation quickly improved his haemodynamic profile, but for the first forty-eight hours he required close monitoring and vasoactive drug support, prompting the acute care team to insert a right internal-jugular double-lumen catheter that remains in situ today for parenteral hydration and high-calorie feeds. Because of persistent abdominal tenderness, low appetite, and generalised fatigue, he has seldom left the bed since admission except with assistance to use a bedside commode, and nursing notes document fewer than two minutes of upright activity in any eight-hour shift. No casts, splints, or traction devices are present, and he recalls no musculoskeletal injuries, falls, or fractures in the current illness. The notebook in his chart indicates that the present operation will be his first trip to an operating room in more than a year, and he underwent no endoscopic or interventional procedures during the thirty days preceding this admission. Past medical records confirm a ten-year history of inflammatory bowel disease affecting the distal small intestine, for which he has been managed as an outpatient on adalimumab every other week; the last biologic dose was administered four weeks before admission. He has never experienced leg pain, asymmetric calf swelling, superficial cord-like veins, or shortness of breath suggestive of venous or pulmonary clot, and duplex ultrasound of the lower limbs performed last year—ordered for mild ankle oedema during steroid taper—was normal. Neither parent nor his two younger siblings has had a thrombotic event or been told of an inherited clotting tendency. He denies chronic lung disease, wheeze, exertional dyspnoea, orthopnoea, or cardiac limitation, and an echocardiogram obtained during a previous flare showed preserved systolic function without valvular abnormality. There is no history of malignancy, myocardial infarction, cerebrovascular accident, spinal cord injury, or connective-tissue disorder. He does not smoke, drinks beer only on weekends when well, and avoids illicit substances. Current medications include piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g every six hours through the central line, adalimumab per schedule, folic acid, and a daily multivitamin; he is not taking corticosteroids, oestrogenic compounds, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or anti-platelet drugs. Review of systems this morning is negative for pleuritic chest pain, productive cough, chills, night sweats, or leg heaviness; he reports ongoing crampy discomfort in the right lower abdomen, controlled with intermittent hydromorphone. On examination he appears pale but attentive, answering questions appropriately. Vital signs recorded fifteen minutes ago show temperature 37.2 °C, blood pressure 118/70 mm Hg, pulse 88 beats per minute regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 97 % on room air; body mass index is 23 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated, the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, and heart sounds are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Breath sounds are vesicular throughout with no crackles or wheeze. The abdomen demonstrates a 6 × 4 cm tender induration in the right iliac fossa overlying the drain site; there is no rebound, and bowel sounds are present. Both lower extremities are warm, of equal circumference, and free of pitting oedema or dilated superficial veins; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ bilaterally, and gentle dorsiflexion of the ankles produces no calf pain. Neurologic screening shows full orientation, intact cranial nerves, and 5/5 strength in the upper limbs, though hip flexion is limited by pain. The central catheter dressing is dry, with no erythema along the tract and brisk blood return on aspiration. Pre-operative laboratory studies drawn through the line at 0600 reveal haemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, haematocrit 35 %, platelets 274 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 8.9 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 0.89 mg/dL, AST 26 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 110 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.3 s with an international normalised ratio of 1.1, and activated partial thromboplastin time 31 s. Twelve-lead ECG shows normal sinus rhythm at 86 bpm with no ST-segment changes, and a portable chest radiograph reviewed at bedside displays clear lung fields with the catheter tip at the cavo-atrial junction. He has been nil per os since midnight; sequential compression sleeves are stocked in the operating theatre and will be applied once anaesthesia has induced general endotracheal anaesthesia, which is expected to last approximately 90 minutes with carbon-dioxide insufflation.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The preoperative Caprini VTE score sums weighted risk factors. The scoring distinction here is how to classify his mobility.
- Crohn disease (inflammatory bowel disease) → 1.
- Sepsis within the past month → 1.
- Indwelling internal-jugular central venous catheter → 2.
- Planned laparoscopic bowel resection lasting >45 minutes → 2.
- Counting his limited mobility with assisted commode transfers as medical bed rest → 1.
Age 30 and BMI 23 add no points. With the 1-point bed-rest classification, the sum is 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1 = 7. If the nine days of minimal mobility are classified as confinement to bed for >72 hours, that criterion scores 2 instead of 1, giving 8.
Final answer: 7
